speechtext:
Oh, I know. I have
caught a few fish out in Saskatchewan and Manitoba and was caught as a fish out there myself too, but by gentlemen of a calibre different from that of the hon. member for Brandon.
I was saying, Mr. Speaker, that we are not in a hopeless mood in the Maritime provinces. In 1867 Nova Scotia had a population of 330,000 and New Brunswick had a population of 252,000. That was our population in those provinces after the lapse of one hundred and twenty years. In the next fifty years the population of Nova Scotia was increased to 523,827 and the population of New Brunswick, I think, to 387,860. In other words in fifty years Nova Scotia increased its population by 59 per cent, while New Brunswick increased its population by 54 per cent. Down there we are sometimes faced with serious problems as the people of other parts of Can-ade are. Nevertheless speaking as a Nova Scotian I want to see the great bulk of our population happy and contented. And they are going to be happy and contented. I do not believe you can find any fair-minded, thinking man in the province of Nova Scotia to-day who will see in secession any brighter days for that province than we have enjoyed and are still going to enjoy under confederation. The papers some time ago spoke of the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey) as a secessionist, which simply goes to show that when the public journals get an idea they broadcast it very freely irrespective in some instances, of whether it is right or wrong. The hon. member for Springfield is no more of a secessionist than I am. He is a broadminded Canadian, a gentleman who has come to our shores and who has made good and will continue to make good. Speaking as a Canadian we invite millions of men of the mental and* physical capacity of the hon. member to our shores.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear. You cannot get them, they are not made.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
So far as I am personally concerned I shall persuade my foe" robust little Canadians to go on singing "O Canada, .we stand on guard for thee." Let every father in Canada teach his children the same

The Budget-Mr. Hocken
refrain and we will have in this country in a few years, notwithstanding the present rivers and floods of pessimism, a very contented people. We have our problems but they are not insurmountable. We can solve them, we must solve them. We have the Crains, we have the muscle, we have the driving force, and we have the intellectual vigour to enable us to do so. We have great natural resources, we have a wonderful country, and if we need capital we can get it both at home and abroad. What we want in order to develop in this Dominion is a tone of optimism and a feeling of broad Canadian patriotism. Speaking for the people of the province from which I come I think I can say till! we have no fears for the future; it looks bright to us.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I join with my hon. friend who has just spoken in deploring the illness and absence of the Minister of Finance. I particularly deplored his absence last session, because I am convinced that if he had been here at that time we would not have heard "The death knell of protection" nor "The first crack out of the box." Hon. Mr. Fielding is too experienced in the work of the Finance department to have taken steps to frighten capital as was done in last year's budget. Ever since that budget was presented there has been a diffidence and a fear on the part of capital to invest in industrial enterprises which has brought us to our rather desperate industrial position.
Mr. Speaker, we have been told on several occasions that the policy of this government is "Wait and see." So far as the present budget is concerned I think I might add this much. "Wait and see, but we will not let you see it all." because the annual statement has been brought down before the end of the fiscal year. That being the case an accurate accounting of the year's business cannot be made. Instead of being provided with exact figures we are driven to estimates, and naturally these estimates have been prepared m accordance with the necessities of the government at the time. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that is an absolutely improper thing for the government to do. The national government should be an example to all business men in the country; and if any business man, or any incorporated company, prepared its annual statement in the way Canada's annual statement has been prepared for this House, that man, or that company, at least, would be liable to heavy penalties. The laws of the provinces of Canada would not permit estimated statements from incorporated companies. But this government I suppose, Sir, is above the law, and it tries to hoodwink the people by the methods that have been adopted. However, I do not think it will succeed. I, at least, will do what I can to show the people of Canada the way the government, in some particulars has attempted to hoodwink them. The government has been ably aided by its press, and has sent forth through its principal organ in this country a statement so misleading and inaccurate that I think attention ought to be called to it. In the issue of the Globe following the presentation of the budget, in 48-point type running right across the page, we find the statement that "Canadian taxpayers are $52,800,000 in pocket," the inference being that the government has saved them that amount in some mysterious way. In smaller type I read that this has been accomplished in the face of big reductions in taxation. I should like some person to tell me in what way taxation was reduced last year. In what way have taxes been reduced so as to account for the placing of this $52,000,000 in the pockets of the people? I take up the statement of the Acting Finance Minister (Mr. Robb) and I find that the loss of revenue consists chiefly in a reduction in the amount received from excise taxes,-the sales tax, the stamp tax and the receipt tax. Any person who can argue that that is a saving to the people of this country must have a very peculiar kind of mind. It indicates clearly that the volume of business transacted in this country was some hundreds of millions of dollars less last year than the year before. If that is an evidence of prosperity to any man's mind I submit he ought to take a course in elementary arithmetic and get some little understanding of business methods. The government has not reduced taxation. This government is imposing higher taxation to-day than has ever been imposed in the Dominion of Canada in all its history. It has a sales tax of five per cent against a sales tax of three per cent when it came into power. It raised the tax to six per cent and pretty nearly ruined the country, then reduced it to five [DOT] per cent, and in addition to that it has imposed a stamp tax on receipts, which is an onerous and irritating tax upon the business of this country. So that, Mr. Speaker, instead of a reduction in taxation, we have an increase in taxation, and yet the journalistic representatives of this government have the mendacity to set out with the largest type they possess that'the people are fifty two million dollars in pocket. The Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) did not say anything like that.
The Budget-Mr. Hocken

I do not think he would dare to say that, because he has a personal reputation to sustain. Indeed we have been informed this afternodn that he is something more than that. He is a superman. I admit cheerfully his agreeable qualities, and I have very high respect for his integrity, and therefore I am satisfied he would not be a party to such statements as have been made in the chief Liberal organ of the Dominion, a statement intended I verily believe to mislead, because I cannot conceive of any responsible newspaper man being in the position to write headings for a paper like the Toronto Globe being so dull of intellect as to imagine he could get away with a thing like that.
Much is made of the fact that the government claims a surplus. These c'aims of surpluses have been made by every legislature and every government we have had since confederation, and thes^ are susceptible as a rule of many interpretations; but this is a very modest surplus, $1,800,000. It has to be observed that it is obtained by unwarranted estimates of the revenue for the present month, for if the revenues of the present month had been kept down to the average for the year, instead of showing a surplus they would have shown a deficit. This government says there is a surplus of $1,800,000, and it adds to that $4,000,000 of interest due from a frozen loan. Roumania and Greece owe to this country many millions of dollars. They have not paid the interest on it, and the interest now amounts to $4,000,000, a substantial sum, and the government has the audacity to say that this $4,000,000 which has been unpaid over a period of years is an asset. They do more than that, Mr. Speaker, they call it revenue.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: A new asset.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
A new asset. They call
it revenue, but 'they have not got it. Revenue is something you have, something that has been paid, but they put it in as revenue, added it to the surplus and make the surplus $5,800,000. I am afraid my hon. friends are following the example of the late managers of the Home Bank, They capitalized the interest on frozen loans, and that is what led them into trouble, and their eventual insolvency. We only have to carry this process a little further, up to a certain point where our natural resources will not suffice, and oui assets will not be sufficient to meet the increased debt charges, then we will be as insolvent as the Home Bank. I have great confidence in the people of this country, and I do not think we are going that far, be-

cause I am looking forward in the course oi the year, or possibly the next year, to the people changing their board of directors, and then we will have no more of this unpaid interest on frozen loans charged u>p to assets and revenues.
The government also makes a serious misstatement when it tells the country that the debt has been increased by thirteen million dollars. WTell, it is something to have them admit that much. They might have added to the estimate of current revenues and reduced that a few million more, butt they apparently went as far in that direction as they thought it*was wise to go. But if we take the operations for the year we will find that, instead of the debt having increased thirteen million, it has increased a hundred and five millions. I will tell hon. members how it is made up and I will challenge anyone to deny the accuracy of my statement. Loans were made to the Canadian National Railway amounting to $S2,000,000.	Every
* bond has the guarantee of this government, and it is as much a national bond as if the name of the National Railway did not appear upon it at all. The credit of the country is pledged to meet those bonds to the extent of $82,000,000. Then we have an over-estimate of this month's revenue of at least $6,000,000. The minister estimates the revenue during March as $35,000,000. He has no warrant whatever for doing that. The fair thing to have done would have been to divide the year's revenue by twelve, and if he had done that he would have found hiis estimate $29,000,000 instead of $35,000,000. but he has added the revenue for this month which cannot be accurately revealed by any person until the end of the month, and has brought down his budget before absolute accuracy could be obtained. By that peculiar process-rather I think discreditable process-he has secured what he has presented as an asset of $6,000,000. I submit that will have to be added to the national debt, and the overdue interest of $4,000,000 which is an addition to the national debt and he has admitted $13,000,000. That makes altogether $105,000,000 which has been added to the debt of the country during the present year. I submit the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) has offended seriously, first in capitalizing debts and calling them assets, and secondly in making excessive estimates of revenues to bolster up an annual statement which might have remained until he had presented it with the accurate figures.
I wonder, Sir, what any banker would say to a client who presented his annual state-

The Budget-Mr. Hocken
meat as the Acting Minister of Finance has presented bis statement to this House, who laid before his banker an annual statement that was based on estimates of the last month's business. I have not a very extensive experience with bankers, but such as I have had leads me to the conclusion that the banker would say to me, " Mr. Hocken, you had better seriously and materially reduce your discounts. Your credit will be curtailed. A statement of this kind does not 'warrant us in giving you the credit we have been giving you in the past." Therefore, from the standpoint of the finances and the debt of this country, it is quite evident that the rosy reports that the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) has presented to the House are not warranted by the facts. I go so far as to say that this taxation, and largely the taxation of this parliament, is strangling the business of this country It is proved in the return, in the fact that $35,000,000 less was collected this year than last year on excise account. There is no better indication of the state of business than the amount paid in sales tax, stamp tax and receipt tax. It is the most accurate barometer of business that can be j reduced. That reduction of $35,000,000 convicts the government of having imposed taxation that is altogether too heavy to 'be borne, and that it is resulting in a substantial decrease in the business of the country. It will be a great disappointment to business throughout Canada that there is no reduction in the soles tax this year. It is an impost that is hard to be borne, and it has ramifications of the most serious character upon general business.
I thought I would draw up, for the edification of the House and the special consideration of the Acting Minister of Finance, a list of taxes that business has to bear in my province, and 1 presume the same is true of other provinces. Every business man is under ton cifierent taxes. He has ten different levies to meet upon his business. From the federal government he has the income tax, cheque tax, receipt tax and sales tax. From ihe provincial government he has the workmen's compensation tax and now he is to have a gasoline tax. In case that might 'be thought to be a trivial affair, there are not very large businesses in Toronto where the managers estimate that the gasoline tax means $1,000 a year in additional taxation. Those are six. Then, of course, he has the ordinary municipal taxation, real property, business tax, income tax and a frontage tax.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Does the tax apply
to gasoline used for commercial purposes?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It applies to gasoline used for all purposes, because the tax is levied at the point of sale. There can be no differentiation between consumers.
Mr. MANION. The farmers are to be exempted.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes. The danger of all
this is that these taxes have to be added to the cost of production. My hon. friends will say that this is passed on to the consumer. No doubt most of it is.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I think the hon member
has neglected to mention the customs tax.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member can add the customs tax if he likes. I am citing direct taxes. These taxes are imposed and extensive statements have to be made with regard to all of them, so that this is .another tax really because the labour involved by chartered accountants preparing these statements is a matter of heavy cost to a business of .any .size. Industry pays a larger proportion of the customs tax than any other portion of the people of Canada. But what I was referring to was direct taxation enforced upon business, which taxation has to be taken out of the receipts, and which makes it so difficult to do business. I know these taxes may 'be .passed on to the consumer, but that makes the purchasing power of consumers in the -cities that much less. It makes the product that the industry produces not only higher in price but smaller .in volume, and this again increases the price. These taxes increase the cost of living. We -are always talking about the cost of living. Everything that increases the cost of production of any article in general consumption must increase the cost of living. But these taxes also seriously embarrass trade in all its ramifications, and they make competition with the United States that much more difficult. My hon. friends have been reading the papers and they will know there have been substantial reductions in taxation in the United States. The aim of their President, Mr. Coolidge, is to reduce taxation to a per capita t-his year of $25. In the Dominion of Canada last year the taxation was $47 per capita. That is an additional burden upon the industry of this country and this adds to the difficulty of competing with the industries of the United States. It will not do to put that aside and say:	That is
immaterial; it does not count. It is one of the things that hampers industry in Canada
The Budget-Mr. Hocken

and that causes a great deail of trouble. It is leading to the economic penetration of the United States into the business of this country. I wonder if my hon. friends know to what extent that is going on? Business after business, some old-established concerns, are being taken over by American capital. We have one in Toronto, a business that was in operation, as I ican recall, when I was five years of age. That is a good while for a business to be in operation, and it has grown to be the largest of its kind in this country I refer to the Christie-Browni Biscuit Com-' pany. That biscuit company is being taken over by the International Biscuit Company of the United States, a biscuit trust. That is only one example of 'the economic penetration by United States capital into the business affairs of this Dominion. It is a serious thing because, when the capital of one nation acquires control of the industry of another, it is then in a position seriously to injure that particular nation. It is not a safe proposition for any country, especially one the size of Canada, to be subject economically to a country like the United States and to have all the capital for the conduct of its industries supplied from that source. It would be a thousand times better for us if we had that capital supplied from Great Britain, with which country we are so closely related. I would not object to that so much, but I do not want the stars and stripes to wave over the biscuit factories or the factories of any other industry of this country. I have had letters recently from men doing business in Wall street, New York, drawing roy attention to the extent to which American capital is invading this country and getting control of its industries, amd I have been invited to express my opinion as to the future of Canada under those circumstances, because in financial circles in New York, as I am informed, this is regarded as simply a prelude to the political penetration of Canada by the United States. I am offering that, not as my opinion, 'but as that of a man who is doing business in the financial district of New York. At all events, I think it must be admitted by every person that it is a serious thing for Canada to have our industries controlled more largely than they are now by capital from the United States.
The result of all this excessive taxation is a general depression in industry which reacts on all classes of the community.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman contend that it is the excessive taxation in this country that is bringing American capital here?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am contending that the excessive taxation makes it difficult to carry on business.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It would be the same for
the British capitalist.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I should be better satisfied to see British capitalists come here. Would the hon. member just as soon have American capital controlling Canadian industry?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have been trying to follow the drift of the hon. member's argument. I do not see what difference it makes whether we have British or American capital so far as taxation is concerned; they would both have to pay the taxes. Personally I am at one with the hon. member in this, that I would rather see British capitalists come here.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Quite so. Now, the Canadian company finds it difficult to continue, and it falls into the hands of an international trust under which it can be operated cheaper than it can if conducted as a separate Canadian industry. I do not mean to say it will suffer any less from taxation because it is in American hands, but these large aggregations of capital controlling Canadian industry and operating under an American trust make it possible for them to carry on where Canadian industry would be unable to exist.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman say why so much Canadian capital finds its way into foreign countries? Take for 5 p.m. instance the financing of the sugar industry in Cuba and the tractor industry of Brazil, and so on.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
One of the faults I have
to find with the present taxation is that Canadian capital will not go into industry. It gets from government guaranteed bonds of the National railways, at 5 per cent, a better return than it can receive from industry. And the capital invested in the industries of this country is at the mercy of further increases in taxation, which all makes it more difficult to operate.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Is the hon. member aware
that there is $900,000,000 of Canadian capital invested free of taxation as a result of the financing of the party he himself supported?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There are government
bonds exempted from taxation to that extent, yes. But I wonder how much of that is held in the United States. These big .fortunes in the United States have been going into tax-free bonds at a rate to excite public attention over there on the part of the press. It is

The Budget-Mr. Hocken
regarded there as a serious thing, and these great aggregations of capital in the United States have purchased a large proportion of this $900,000,000 of Canadian bonds.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not a very large proportion.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How much?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My information is that the
great bulk is held in Canada.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is broad. Let us
take the case of a Canadian capitalist who is able to put his money into tax-free Canadian bonds at 5 per cent. If he put that money into anything else he would have to pay 30, 40 and 50 per cent income tax, whereas taking a low rate of interest on tax-free bonds he can still be a lot ahead.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I admit that.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
And the money is being
withheld from the development of industries; it is withheld from the development of our natural resources, by reason of the excessive taxation imposed upon it. I submit to the minister that in the circumstances there is nothing which this country needs so much to-day as a reduction in taxation. We cannot compete alongside the United States unless we have lower taxes. The present excessive taxation is seen in the general depression of industry and business, and we have that fully set out in the figures that have been submitted. We have for instance some $35-
676,000	less collected in excise taxes than the year before; there is a shrinkage in business as represented by these figures. But the undue taxation is also seen in the departure of so many native-born Canadians to the United States to obtain employment.
My hon. friend (Mr. Forke) speaking the other night told us that the policy of the present government, as he understood it, was to reduce the cost of the necessities of life. Well, I thought while the hon. gentleman was .speaking that the government had certainly succeeded in reducing one important necessity, and I will give them credit to that extent. They have undoubtedly succeeded in reducing what I consider to be the prime necessity of life, the one upon which all other necessities rest, and that is wages. The government have succeeded in reducing wages in this country. The pay envelope in Cape Breton is reduced to three days a week and it is the same in other parts of the country, while in some cases there is no pay envelope at all. So that the government is entitled to that much credit, and I freeljr accord it.
But not only are our people drifting over the line; unemployment has got to such a stage as to tax the resources of private charity, as well as the revenues of our municipalities. This government takes no responsibility for the unemployed; that is a matter that is not in the British North America Act. Private charity is obliged to take care of these people, and evangelists are opening soup kitchens and giving free lunches in our city. And the municipality is spending thousands weekly maintaining a house of industry. Every police station of the city is crowded each night with men who are unable to find any other place in which to lie. Not for years within my recollection have the police stations been so flooded with men who wanted be is as they have been during the past year. Now there is only one way to remedy this situation and that is by lower taxation, a little more encouragement for the industries to keep these men employed. I find no mention of these problems in the budget; they are treated as nonexistent, and I am afraid that the government is not inclined to give to such matters the attention they deserve.
It is all right to talk optimism. Every little while someone who is properly heeled himself, who has a good salary, a man who perhaps is living under the protection of a public institution, makes a public speech to a Canadian club and says, "Let us be optimists". That is all right in a way; and there is no more pronounced optimist in this country than I am. But when a man has an empty stomach and nothing at all in his pocket, when he has no prospect, no bed, it is pretty hard to maintain that optimism. A man who is an optimist under these circumstances is certainly equal to that celebrated character in one of Dickens' books who thought it was a credit to himself to 'be cheerful only under the most a 'verse conditions that could possibly exist.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mark Tapley.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That's the gentleman. It was only when he was trodden down into the ground that he felt he had a right to bn proud of his cheerfulness. But it is pretty hard for a man whose stomach is empty to be optimistic. I have great faith in Canadians. I have seen them come through hard t-mes. I have seen them tighten their belts when they could easily take up another hole in the belt without stretching it very much. On more than one occasion we have found our way back to prosperity.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
How about the reduction on grape fruit?

The Budget-Mr. Hocken

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Grape fruit is not very filling unless you eat the peel, and I do not know how that would agree with one's digestion. I have noticed that the usual way the people of this country return to prosperity is by way of the ballot, and I do not think that test can now be long deferred. That makes me feel optimistic.
This government seem to think that the highest type of statesmanship is to discover new sources of taxation. Instead of practising rigid economy, reducing the cost of government in every particular, they go along with no apparent effort in that direction. During the past year 1,572 new employees were appointed by the Civil Service Commission at the request of the government. Surely that is an excessive number to add to the service if the government are really desirous of reducing its cost.
I am glad, Mr. Speaker, to see that agriculture is prosperous. I am glad to see that agricultural products are commanding high prices. But I would like to see the market gardener, for whom the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) spoke yesterday, prosperous as well as the grain grower. I would like to see the constituents of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) a little more prosperous, because he represents a market garden constituency too. All along lake Erie and in the southern counties bordering on lake Ontario there are market gardens, and I regard the people who are engaged in this work as agriculturists. I do not know what my hon. friends to my left would call them; but they are working the land; they are providing the things that the people want. But by reason of the present tariff the appetite of the public for these products is satiated before the products of our own market gardeners come in. The hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) says that is the fault of the climate; you cannot beat the climate, therefore we cannot do anything to help it. But something could be done to heilp it. If a tax were put on these early vegetables, particularly the early fruits, then the people who wanted them could pay the tax; the country would get the revenue, and the people who are growing these things in Canada would also benefit.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would my hon. friend advocate that?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Most assuredly I advocate it. I advocate higher duties on market garden produce and early fruits, with three cheers and a tiger.
[Mr. Charters.l
The government, Mr. Speaker, have acted like a body of men fearful of every step they take. The budget makes no decreases in duties because of the east, and no increases in duties because of the farmers of the west; so the government stand pat. They are like a lady who walks down one of our Ottawa streets on these slushy days and picks her steps very warily for fear her feet will get wet. But capital in this country has no confidence in the present government. The real Finance minister-the sick Finance minister, rather-would not have frightened capital as it was frightened last year by at least three members of the government. He would not have put capital in the position of being fearful of investment. On the contrary, I think he would have done what he had promised to do, maintain a stable tariff. He would thereby have incurred, perhaps, the disapproval of my hon. friends to my left, but his knowledge of affairs and his experience-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
They have seen the error
of their way.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes; the experience and
the judgment and the ability, represented by the Minister of Finance, lay on a sick bed, and they saw the error of their way. They not only made reductions in the tariff, but they frightened to death anyone who could understand what was meant by "the first crack out of the box."
There is another matter to which I want to refer, namely, the export tax on power. Before dealing with that, however, I would like to suggest that if the government really wanted to encourage industry in this country; if they wanted to enable the country to get the maximum benefit from its natural resources, they might have put an export tax on pulpwood, or if you like, an embargo on pulpwood. There is nothing I can think of that would so certainly add to the industrial wealth of Canada, without in the slightest degree requiring a tariff, as the development of the paper making industry here. We allow our wood to be cut down and sent out as wood, by the cord, getting for it what is a mere trifle, instead of taking the legitimate and self-preserving method of saying, "This is a great natural resource of this country, and we are going to have it manufactured here; we are going to send out the finished product or we Shall not send it out at all." If the government took that stand, paper mills would be established all over the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, and the favourable baJlanoe of trade would be very materially increased.

The Budget-Mr. Hocken

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would that not likely be United States capital?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If it was United States
capital the pay envelope would go to Canadian workmen, and the Canadian grooer would get his trade, the Canadian shoemaker would get his trade and the Canadian farmer would get his trade.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I thought the hon. gentleman was afraid of United States capital.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am not so sure it would be all United States capital. British capital is available for sure-fire industries, and there is no reason why others than the Sturgeon Palls mill, which is operated by British capital, should not be established on a similar basis all over the two provinces. You can only keep our own population at home by giving them work, and when you give them work and let them earn good wages, as paper mill men do, then you have a state of general prosperity for the merchant, for the farmer and for everyone concerned-even for the banker, although my hom. friends to my left do not care very much about him.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I see by your own paper that they are coming home.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Does my hon. friend deny there is a substantial exodus to the United States

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, but they
are coming home raider this government, I am glad to see.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
How many are coming
home?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: In the last month, 44,044.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
And 160,000 went away in the same period. If that is the kind of exchange that is going on, and if my hon. friend is satisfied with it, I beg to say that I am not.
I want to say a few words, Mr. Speaker, on the tax on power. This will produce a revenue, we are told, of $400,000. Well, $200,000 of that tax will be paid by the municipalities of Ontario. lit will not be paid by those who use the power, because the power contracts that exist in the province of Ontario are for long periods, and it has been necessary for the municipalities to take over those contracts when they took over the plants which are providing the power sent across the line. The municipalities own those plants. The Toronto Power Company and the Ontario Power Company together are sending out 103i
approximately 100,000 horse-power. They
must continue to send it dut at the price they are now getting, and all that this tax means is that the consumers of power in Ontario will have to pay this $200,000 to the Dominion government. If the idea were to exact a tax and get some revenue from one of our natural resources sent out of the country-and I cannot conceive of any other reason-then it absolutely fails so far as the province of Ontario is concerned, because, as I say, these contracts exist and must be carried on for a considerable period by the municipalities that own these plants. But that is not the material objection. I want to say and I venture to assert, Mr. Speaker, that the time will come when what I say now will be recalled in this House. A real act of statesmanship, so far as this power is concerned, would be to place an embargo on the export of power. I do not know, and I do not care, whether anybody else in this House agrees with me, but I am prepared to stand by that proposition, because in my opinion it is one of the most important that faces Canada. Twenty years ago electrical power meant nothing to the people of this country. It was used in small quantities then, but since that time, and coming down to to-day, hydro-electric energy has become a commodity that is required in practically every home and every municipality and every industry, and for this country, which has a large quantity, and can develop much larger quantities, to go on exporting that power when it is as certain as that day follows night that in a short time we will be wanting it for our own purposes is a policy that I think is about as stupid as anything that could be adopted.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
May I ask the hon.
member if there is any loss in that power now going out? Will not the power be there next year, or has it gone forever once it has crossed the line?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
When that power is once
exported it is practically gone forever. No man in the United States will make a contract for power unless it is for so long that at the end of that period it will be impossible for this country to recover its power. The cost of installation for the use of large units of power is so great that nobody on the other side could afford to invest capital in such an enterprise unless a continuous supply of power was assured over a long period.
There is a proposition for the development of power now at Carillon Falls. According to information that I have, they will develop there 400,000 horse-power, and only 100,000
The Budget-Mr. Hocken

of that horse-power is to be reserved for the use of the people of Canada. Three hundred thousand horse-power of the amount developed at that point is to be exported to the United States, and it is to be exported on a twenty-five year agreement.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Where does my hon. friend
get that information? What is the basis for making that statement?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I got it out of one of the newspapers. That is the common talk. It was stated in the city of Quebec yesterday.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The government have not
heard of it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There are a great many
things the government do not hear of first. There is no doubt they are developing the power there.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
So far as I know they have
not put a pick in it yet. They have not got a contract.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
They have not got a contract? Well, it has been talked of for some time, and it has come down to definite propositions and definite figures in the press of yesterday; I am quoting from the press of yesterday. However, I am quite content, if it suits my hon. friend, to let that go, and I will make my argument on something else.
It may be argued that an embargo on power would offend the United States because it is an unusual proceeding to take. But the conditions are unusual with regard to power. Power is not like any other natural resource. It occupies a position all by itself. I want to point out that if an embargo is not put on now, an effective embargo cannot be put on later. After we have exported, and are exporting, large quantities of power to the United States for a considerable period, it will be impossible for us then to put an embargo on the export of power without grave international complications. While the United States might be offended at such an act on our part to-day, they would have much greater right to be offended if we took that action after a lapse of twenty or twenty-five years, when we discovered that we had made a mistake and wanted to undo it. I submit, Sir, that electric power generated by water is the greatest of all our natural resources. It is something that is perpetual. It is not like a mine that can be dug out, and then it is done; but it is something that runs on perpetually, and is of such a peculiar quality that there is no other natural resource the nation has to compare with it. It affords us in the Dominion of Canada perhaps the

most substantial hope of successful competition with the United States in industry. Cheap power to a large industry is an important consideration, and with Canada possessing the tremendous volume that it does to-day we will be in a position as we develop to compete with the United States on a lower duty than would otherwise be the case, because this will act as some measure of protection.
Power is a commodity which is used in almost every phase of community life to-day. The municipalities add to the pleasures and comfort of life by electric lighting, and by the use of power for their municipal services, and in many other ways. It is used all over any city where there are elevators. It is used in industries so that western Ontario has become practically a hive of industry, with large developments since this power was available for industrial purposes. It has facilitated the growth of industry in western Ontario to a greater degree than any other single factor, and it is providing in our homes, and upon our farms-in farm homes as well as in city and town homes-conveniences for the wife, for the husband and for the whole family. There is nothing that touches the lives of our people more intimately to-day, financially, socially and municipally than this tremendous asset that we have, and for that reason I submit that it should not be exported.
Let me just indicate to my friends what a development there has been during the last few years. I take you back only about two years to the installation of the Chippawa plant when the first generator was installed- only two years and yet 400,000 horse-power is being generated now. Every horse-power is sold and the people are clamouring for more. There is a demand for more power notwithstanding that big development. That has not gone into industry because I venture to say there is less power being used by industries in western Ontario to-day than there was two years ago. There are fewer industries working and nonei of them are working double time. That has all gone into the homes and into the municipalities, into making life more pleasant and agreeable to the people of our country. I deduce from that, Mr. Speaker, that if we had a million horse-power developed in this province it would not be very long before every horsepower would be in demand in Ontario, and it would be used for the benefit of industry and for the benefit of the people in every walk of life.
I think we are only at the beginning of the advantages to be obtained from the generation and distribution of this wonderful new

The Budget-Mr. Hocken
agency of civilized life. I do not think any person can stand here to-day and forecast the future. In the future more electrical power will be needed in this Dominion if we can estimate from the experience of the past. We only have to go back about twenty years when Mr. P. W. Ellis, of Toronto, and Mr. Patinson of Brantford, made their first investigation as to whether it would be feasible to develop power at Niagara Falls and sell it to the people of Ontario. That is not more than twenty years ago, and while I have not got the figures- I venture to say that there is a million horse-power being generated and sold in the province of Ontario to-day. If that has been our experience in the last twenty years what is going to be our experience in the next two decades? And have we not a right to look further than the next twenty years? Have we not the right to try and get a vision of the future needs of this country and prepare for them, protect those future needs by what we do to-day?
So far as my own province is concerned this export tax is not serious. It means $200,000 to the municipalities but I guess they can stand that better than they can stand some other things. I do not know that an export tax is going to hurt the province of Ontario seriously, but it may be different with the province of Quebec under the conditions that exist in this country to-day. I have no particular brief for the province of Quebec, except that I like to see every part of our country prospering to the highest degree possible. But I should like to try and convince my hon. friends who represent that province that they are in a dangerous position with regard to the export of power, and they need an embargo many times worse than does the province of Ontario. In the latter province the provincial government has given the municipalities control of the power developments, and they will control those power developments in the future. The province of Ontario, fortunately, is in a position to protect itself against the export of power, and all the power that is generated within its precincts will be used for the benefit of the people and for the development of industry in the province. But the conditions are different in the province of Quebec. There the legislature has been somewhat short-sighted; they never caught the vision of the public ownership of the generation and distribution of power, and all the power developments are now in the hands of private capital. I am not going to discuss the wisdom or otherwise of that except to point out that it
leaves the province of Quebec in a hopeless plight so far as the preservation of its power is concerned unless there is an embargo. If the embargo is not put on until 50 or 75 per cent of the power generated in Quebec has been sold then the restriction will be impossible. What will be the result? That this great agent for industrial development, this extremely valuable accessory of the development of industry will be denied to the province of Quebec; it will be enjoyed by the adjoining province to the west.

speechtext: Mr. PIUS MICHAUD (Restigouche and Madawaska) moved the second reading of Bill No. 33 respecting The Restigouche Log Driving and Boom Company.

subtopic: THE RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: THE RESTIGOUCHE LOG DRIVING AND BOOM COMPANY
speechtext:
This company was incorporated by act of the legislative assembly of New Brunswick in 1879, and by chapter 155 of the statutes of Canada 1910 the name was changed from The Restigouche Log Driving Company to The Restigouche Log Driving and Boom Company. The petitioners were incorporated, and chapter 155 of the statutes of Canada provides, as regards the powers of the company, as follows, in section (28):
The company may construct, acquire, charter, navigate and maintain tugs, boats, dredges and other craft for towing logs and for other use in and about the said booms, and also may, for its own use, construct, acquire and operate telegraph, telephone and electric light lines in connection with its business and works upon the Restigouche river.
Section (29) provides:
The directors may issue bonds of the company to the extent of $150,000 par value, which bonds shall be a first lien upon all the plant, property, assets, rights, credits and revenues of the company and upon all logs being the property of the members of the company, irom year to year handled by the company while such logs are in the possession of the company or under its control, and shall be secured thereby.
Under the present legislation, it is provided:
Cl) In addition to the bonds authorized by chapter lo5 of the statutes of 1910, the directors of The Restigouche Log Driving and Boom Company (hereinafter called "the Company") may issue bonds (hereinafter called "renewal bonds") of the company, not exceeding in the whole the sum of $150,000 par value. The directors may, at any time, issue a part of such renewal bonds equal, in the aggregate, to the par value of those of the bonds authorized by said Chapter 155

The Budget-Mr. MacLean (Prince)
(hereinafter called "old bonds") which have matured and have heretofore been paid by the company, and hereafter, as and when any old bond or old bonds mature and are paid by the company, the directors may issue in place thereof respectively a renewal bond or itnewal bonds, from time to time, for an amount or amounts, not exceeding the par value of any such old bond or bonds so maturing.
The bill further provides:
Any such renewal bonds so issued to replace any old bond or bonds which have heretofore been paid by the company or which shall hereafter be paid by the company, shall be distributed pro rata to and amongst all those persons, firms and corporations who, as members of the company in the fiscal year in which any such old bond or bonds have been or shall be paid, have contributed, or shall contribute by tolls, or assessments towards the payment of eabh of such old bonds. Such renewal bonds shall be distributed to such persons, firms and corporations in the proportion that the amount paid by each such person, firm or corporation to the company for tolls, or assessments in such fiscal year bears to the total amount received by the company from its members therefor in such year.
What the petitioners desire is a renewal of the old bonds.

Mr. Speaker, when the House rose at six o'clock I was referring to the financial situation and I had outlined some of the deficits that had been left by the previous government. I may be permitted to analyze briefly the cause of some of those deficits incurred under the regime of our hon. friends opposite. I made some reference to the consolidation of the interest which was due on the loan to Roumania and Greece. I think we can congratulate this government on attempting to do something to have this account put in a satisfactory condition. As you will remember, this loan was made at a time when the financial resources of Canada were taxed to
their very utmost. Our friends who are today so critical of the country's finances seemed to be reckless of them at that time and were willing to plunge in and spend money in almost any way that could be found. In fact one would almost imagine they were looking for some channels into which they could turn the public moneys of Canada. In that connection I wish to refer briefly to Hansard of May 18, 1921, and to a speech made by the hon. member for Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Archambault) on that day. He said:
I now come to a very interesting matter and one with which I dealt to some extent last year, I mean the credits extended by the government to Greece and Roumania. Although I spoke upon this question last year there have been some further developments, and I believe I shall be able to convince you, Sir, that the high standard of political morality in this country has remained unimpaired according to certain mentalities that we find in this House. Sir, in our efforts to probe the morality evidenced in connection with these credits let us examine the whole subject. It will be remembered that in the month of May, 1919, the then Minister of Finance, Sir Thomas White, asked this House to vote these credits because the population of Roumania was starving and needed food; and I can well remember the right hon. gentleman saying at that time, "Will the population of Canada remain unmoved and not help the population of Roumania which is now starving?" Well, Sir, two credits of $25,000,000 each were opened, one for Roumania and one for Greece. Of this amount, $26,989,000 has already gone and only $3,500,000 has been spent on food.
This very small loan, out of $50,000,000, was all that our hon. friends were able to spend on foodstuffs for the starving people of Roumania; and you will note, Mr. Speaker, that that was the excuse for granting the loan. I quote further:
The hon. member for Megantic (Mr. Pacaud) said the other night that the government of Canada, in answer to a merchant in Belgium who asked that food should be exported from these moneys, said that only one-fifth of the credit to Belgium could be devoted to the purchase and exportation of food. Now, Sir, a return was brought down last year to an order of the House-I refer to "Sessional Paper No. 147." This return shows conclusively that companies controlled by the Minister of Marine (Mr. Ballantyne), the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Lalor), the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt), the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin) and the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Elkin) had sold goods for export which had been paid for by the government. I was under the impression that the disclosures of last year would have had their effect and that there would not be a repetition of any such transactions; but although since April 19, the government of Roumania has defaulted in two or three payments of interest, and probably Greece also, more of this money has been going to favourites of the government, and a further sum of $5,342,077.32 has been advanced. The Budget-Mr. MacLean (Prince)
Coming to the amendment that was moved by the hon. the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) the other day, I notice that one of the first items he mentioned in his amendment is the sales tax. He says:
Conditions in Canada urgently demand reductions of taxation, especially of the sales tax and other levies which have been increased by the present government; the House regrets that the financial statements now presented show no evidence of the economy necessary to make such reductions possible, but rather disclose an alarming increase in the public debt.
My hon. friend refers in the first instance to the sales tax. I wish to submit a statement in that connection to show that there was a loss of revenue due directly to the reduction in the sales tax of last year.
The decrease in revenue this year is estimated to amount to about $52,800,000 brought about by a decrease in customs duties collected of about $13,300,000, a decrease of excise taxes of $35,676,000, the chief source of this tax being the sales tax and a decrease of about $2,353,000 from delayed business profits tax. These decreases were offset to some extent by an increase of about one million dollars in excise duty and about $2,300,000 in income taxes collected.
The revenue of this country, which is estimated to be about 344 million dollars, is taxation, and it is evident that a decrease in revenue is a decrease in taxation. Our estimated population at present is about 9,225,000. Therefore, this decrease in taxation means a saving in taxes of about $5.75 per head for each man, woman and child in this country.
This was brought about by reducing the duties on agricultural implements and on the materials imported for the manufacture of these implements, and by removing the sales tax from all the articles and materials consumed in the process of manufacture of these agricultural implements, as well as by reducing the sales tax from 6 to 5 per cent. Like reductions were made in the duty payable on articles relating to the fruit growing industry, poultry industry, dairying industry, mining and quarrying industries, the lumbering and fishing industries. The sales tax was removed also on these articles. The list of exemptions was increased among which we find, binder twine, cream separators and others.
These reductions have no doubt stimulated our Canadian industries, the result, as I have showed, being that we imported 70 million dollars less for the period covered by the eleven months ending February, 1925 than during the eleven months ending February, 1924. Although this meant a loss in revenue of about twenty million dollars, it decreased the burden of taxation on our Canadian people to that
extent, as well as encouraged our Canadian people to supply the decrease in importation by enhancing Canadian production to supply our demands.
So I do not think that the ex-Minister of Finance could very well prove his contention that the sales tax was immaterial, or that the reductions that were effected last year did not mean a reduction in the revenue and also a big reduction in taxation.
I	wish now to refer to another matter which always receives a great deal of attention in this House; I refer to the question of the tariff. I hold in my hand a resolution which has been standing on t'he order paper in the name of the right hon. leader of the opposition since February 5. It starts out by saying:
This Dominion requires an immediate revision of the Canadian tariff on a definitely and consistently protective basis.
So evidently there is no doubt in his mind but that this is the proper course to pursue. Higher protection. He goes on to say:
That such revision should apply to natural products such as farm products, fish, and coal with no less thoroughness than to manufactured goods.
I	would like the hon. gentleman to explain to the House what benefit a protective tariff would be on agricultural products. A protective tariff against goods of which we have a surplus cannot be effective. The hon. gentleman will admit that water cannot rise above its own level, and this is a similar case; American agricultural products cannot come in here unless there is an absolute shortage on the Canadian market. As far as the duty is concerned on American fish coming into Canada, any man in the Maritime provinces or in any other part of Canada who has any knowledge of the fishing industry will admit that the only market in which the Canadian fisherman can obtain remunerative prices for his fish is the American market. Again, I would like any hon. gentleman in this House to point out where American fish is supplanting the Canadian article on the Canadian market. To my mind the mention of fish in this resolution is simply propaganda, an endeavour to appeal to the fishermen. It has really no significance.
If I wished to go into that a little further, I migdi't submit figures to show that the total imports of fresh fish from across the border into the whole of Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific amount to only $364,000, and of this amount, $233,000 is for oysters, or what are known as shelled oysters, which are imported into Canada under a duty of 10 cents per gallon. I leave it to the people

of Canada who consume this article whether in their opinion the policy advocated by the right hon. leader of the opposition in his resolution is in the interests of this country. Those oysters cannot come into the Maritime provinces because they would not be used there even if they were brought in and given away free.
