The few oysters that we do have in the Maritime provinces to ship at the present time find a ready market in the cities of Quebec and Montreal and in the Maritime provinces themselves, so that the word fish in this resolution is pure political propaganda.
The next paragraph refers to the conservation and development of our natural resources. No fault can be found with that, but every member on this side is just as anxious to see our resources properly developed as hon. gentlemen opposite are.
The next paragraph is more or less of a surprise coming as it does from the Conservative party who on different occasions have endeavoured to make the people of this country believe they were the great imperialists and had a monopoly on this side of the water, of patriotism and loyalty to the Motherland. Still we find this paragraph goes so far as to state that hon. gentlemen opposite are in favour of withdrawing the British preference already granted to Great Britain and which is an inducement for goods to come through' Canadian ports. Their excuse for this policy is that it is in the interest of the workers of the country. This again, to my mind, is purely political propaganda and an appeal to the workers and the manufacturing interests of the country. Well, I will venture the assertion that if hon. members opposite were in power to-morrow they would not dare to put such a proposition into effect.
In this connection I think it will be only fair to point out how the existing duty, even under the British preference, affects the Maritime provinces. We have two gentlemen in this House one the member for St. John and Albert (Mr. Baxter) and the other the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Black) who claim to be the champions of the rights of the Maritimes. Let me point out to these gentlemen how this policy of a withdrawal of the British preference would affect the Maritime provinces. Supposing a ship load of goods valued at $100,000 arrives at the port of St. John or the port of Montreal. Immediately that ship docks a crowd of customs officers at once patrol the docks. They pounce upon that ship and even under 
present conditions will ask to have handed over at least $20,000 in duties. Supposing you increase the present duty 10 or 15 per cent and instead of $20,000 the sum demanded would be $35,000. Will hon. friends opposite point out how thev expect the ports of St. John and Halifax to flourish under such a proposition? They cannot answer this argument and the very suggestion would drive business from those ports. As I said before, if they held the reins of power to-morrow they would not dare to put any such proposition into effect. If they did I do not see how the orators of the Conservative party could go to the country and again fool the people by waving the flag of loyalty to the Mother Country.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman advocate taking off all the duties on British goods coming in so as to increase the trade entering Maritime province ports?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is all right for the hon. gentlemen who have not the responsibility of governing the country to advocate a policy of that kind but in view of the financial condition of the country regard must be had to ways and means whereby sufficient revenue can be raised to meet the needs of Canada. Even with the preference as low as it is there has been a greater increase in imports from countries which do not enjoy the preference than there has been in imports from Great Britain.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would that not be all the more reason why we should reduce the duty on British goods still further?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend might be justified in his view but the present arrangement is working out fairly well. The preference already granted has tended to bring goods to Canadian ports. Ninety-nine per cent of the goods imported from Great Britain now come to Canadian ports as a result of the 10 per cent additional preference that was granted last year. I certainly would be in favour of a further increase in the preference if it were at all possible; I am entirely opposed to the proposal of hon. gentlemen opposite to withdraw the preference and I think that when we take that stand the country is behind us.
There is this further fact, and it will perhaps be an effective answer to my hon. friend, that according to official figures the imports from Great Britain in Canada in 1924 actually decreased as compared with the previous year. I do not know how the hon. gentleman can explain that. At the same

The Budget-Mr. MacLean (Prince)
time Canadian exports to Great Britain increased- Nevertheless the protectionist opposition will still argue that the British preference is responsible for admitting into Canada an increasing volume of British goods.
I might further point out that during the same period while imports from Great Britain were decreasing imports from Germany were increasing at an enormous rate on which a high duty is charged. Canada grants no tariff preference to Germany yet that country supplied goods to Canada last year to the value of nearly $6,000,000 as compared with less than $5,000,000 in 1923 and $2,000,000 in 1922. When our friends of the opposition blame the Liberal policy of the British preference for the increased popularity of British goods in Canada they should also explain the reason for the growing volume of German goods to which no tariff preference is accorded. But the expounders of this protectionist policy are in the game for some other purpose than to enlighten the public. They cannot fool the people all the time but they look forward to fooling part of the people part of the time, and in that way to again put something over the Canadian public as they did in 1911.
The next paragraph in this resolution recommends the appointment of a tariff commission. Had that proposition been advanced by the government bon. gentlemen opposite would be the first to utter denunciations because of the appointment of another commission. However-, if the present government did not get better results from the appointment of such a commission than the country obtained from the tariff commission of some years ago over which the ex-Minister of Finance presided the expenditure for the purpose would be a pure waste of money.
The last paragraph in the resolution contains the only sane proposition in the entire list. This has reference to transportation burdens, and suggests that relief be given to the western and Maritime provinces by way of a contribution from the government to reduce freight rates. I should like the House to take notice of that fact: The proposition of the right bon. leader of the opposition is that the western and Maritime provinces be given relief in freight rates by a contribution from the government of Canada. The proposition may be commendable but I cannot see how the originator of the proposition can reconcile that policy with the attitude he is taking with regard to the government's proposed control of ocean freight rates. What he is proposing is absolutely along the same line as the policy of the government
contemplates. Would the right hon. gentleman be good enough to point out to the House and country, what benefit it would be to the producer of the Maritime or western provinces to grant a reduction of rates to Montreal only to find that when the goods arrived there the ocean rates were prohibitive and that the goods could not be exported at a profit. This is something I should like the right hon. gentleman ito explain when he next comes to discuss the Petersen contract.
I	know that hon. gentlemen opposite are quite adept at Changing their position in an endeavour to square themselves with their proposals, but it wild take all the ability of the right hon. leader of the opposition to explain the really ridiculous position in which he finds himself by reading this clause of his resolution.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I should like to draw
attention to the fact that this discussion is wholly out of order, but inasmuch as the hon. gentleman has been debating this resolution for some twenty minutes I trust that hon. gentlemen on this side of the House will also be accorded the privilege of discussing it when they come to reply.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In reply to my
hon. friend let me say that I am quite in order. I understood, when the hon. gentleman did not have a chance ito discuss this resolution on private miemfoer's day, he would have a chance to 'discuss it on the budget, and I am quite sure he will avail himself of the opportunity.
I think I have paid enough attention to this rather peculiar document, and I pause for a moment to draw the attention of the House to another motion, and I only wish I could say that I thought it was prepared by some other member; but unfortunately the members of the House will find that it was prepared by the same hon. gentleman. I find the resolution which I have reference to stood in the name of the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen), who was then the member for Portage la Prairie, and in this connection I wish to read from page 1915 of the Debates of the House of Commons of January 18, 1911. The ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton), in addressing the House in one of his pedantic flights of oratory used the word "wobbled." I think he attributed that to the quality of this government, or possibly some of his friends on this side of the House. I wish to point out that this resolution to which I have just referred, which was submitted by the right hon. leader of

The Budget-Mr. MacLean (Prince)
the opposition which I am about to read, is not wobbling at all. It is worse than that. It is an acrobatic feat which possibly very few of us can perform, and that is a complete somersault, or right about face, or looping the loop, as one hon. member suggests. This resolution of January 18, 1011 reads as follows:
That in the opinion of this House, a substanttial reduction in the import duties on agricultural implements is now due the agriculturists of Canada, and is in just accord with the true ends of a protective tariff.
He then goes on to say:
But the charge I have to make and which I hope to bring home to the government this afternoon is not that one, though it is the most serious; it is this, that in their attempts to continue the National Policy which had obtained for years before, they have overlooked, they have neglected one essential feature of that policy, they have quite forgotten its guiding principle, namely the principle that as our industrial institutions advanced in strength and as they were able with every advance to acquire a hold on the home market, the import duties were to be diminished and adjusted in order to meet the evolving and changing conditions. It is that restraining, guiding principle which I claim this government has entirely overlooked and as a consequence they have allowed, in the respect which I am discussing this afternoon, protection to run rampant, and they have for reasons which are only too obvious become the slaves of those who helped them into power, and who now maintain them there behind ramparts of gold.
And so on all through his speech. The leader of the opposition, the gentleman who proposed this resolution, now asks for a higher protective tariff. The maxim, "consistency thou art a jewel" is correct. I just imagine, if any hon. gentleman on this side of the House placed himself in this ridiculous position, to what flights of oratory our hon. friends opposite would rise in exposing his position to this House and to the country at large. But proceeding on this line a little further, I find that the hon. ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton), speaking on the budget on April 10, 1924, seemed to lament the fact that we were shut out of the American market. He said:
We would further expect something to be done to help the Canadian farmer who to-day is shut out by an absolute barrier from his natural market to the south.
If this statement which the hon. gentleman expressed in the debate last year was correct on April 10, 1924, was it net also correct in 1911, when hon. members opposite shut us out of that market, and shut us out in the Maritime provinces to the detriment of those provinces possibly for all time to come? Yet those hon. members to-day will stand up in this chamber and say:	"The government
should do something to let the Canadian farmer into the market to the south of them, which is their natural right." I think this is
fMr A. E. MacLean.]
so amusing that we can hardly realize that the hon. gentleman would express such sentiments, and as an hon. member suggests, a real and national tragedy was enacted at that time involving the infliction of a great wrong on the people of Canada. Discussing the matter further the ex-Minister of Finance says:
The tariff has nothing to do with the difficulties of the farmer.
He gave us three causes for it, hard times, the practically prohibitive tariff of the United States directed in the main against farm products, the deflation of prices applicable to grain and live stock, and the loss of the purchasing power of the great consuming country due to the war. Here again the hon. gentleman stresses the fact that file United States is our only market, and again I ask, if it was right on April 10, 1924, ivhal was wrong with it in 1911 when our friends, with the assistance of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, diut us out of that market, probably for all time to come?
In this connection I wish to point out to my hon. friends in the section of the House almost directly opposite to me, what the manufacturers' attitude is to-day in regard to this same question, and I quote from the Financial Times of April 10, 1924, shortly after the last budget speech was delivered. This paper is published in Montreal, and the article reads:
The Manufacturers' Association at their meeting stated as follows:	" The future seems clear for an
out-and-out struggle between two ''-
Mark these words:
-" between two, not three, political groups for the maintenance or destruction of the fiscal policy that was brought into effect in 1878."
The Manufacturers' Association realize that the aims and objects of our friends of the Progressive party and of a large majority, I must say, if not all, but, I hope, of all of the Liberal party, are the same, and it is their duty at the next eleotion to go out and fight both the Progressive party and the Liberal party on this issue. The article continues :
It may be that the manufacturers and labour elements in eastern Canada will be forced to take up the gauge. The tariff, unfortunately, has been thrust again into the political arena. The manufacturers must remember, therefore, that it is votes that count, and they must be prepared to justify a protective policy to the electors, to the consumer, if they are to win out in the political fight.
If who is to win out? I ask hon. gentlemen whom this has reference to. Is it any political party that is going to win out? No, they say, if we are going to win out; if the

The Budget-Mr. MacLean (Prince)
Manufacturers' Association are going to win
out! It is their election and they say:	We
must join with the Labour party and go out and defeat those two other parties, the Liberals and the Progressives.
As their official champions in the federal field the Conservative leaders should be prepared to dispense with the extreme exaggerated attitude and statements that set forth their views on the present budget. Mr. Meighen's first interview was hardly the carefully considered, serious, statesmanlike opinion that the country had the right to expect. It too, was strongly tinged with political considerations.
As we have urged before, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, if it enters the fight officially, must make it clear that it holds a reasonable view on " protection," and that it is quite prepared, and, indeed, will insist on periodic revisions of the tariff not only upwards-
Mark those words.
-but in a downward direction where manufacturers are taking advantage of excessive customs duties to bear too heavily on the average consumer. Extreme demands can only alienate support.
Hon. members will notice that they endeavour to camouflage that a little at the last, but let them go out and defeat those two parties at the next election, and I can *assure the people of this country and hon.
members of this House that the 9 pan. revision of the tariff will certainly not be downwards, but be upwards with a vengeance. I do not know whether I am within my rights or not, but I am going to take a long shot at it and say that whoever sees another campaign fought in this country will see the money which has been extracted from the pockets of the consumers by the Manufacturers' Association thrown into that campaign to defeat the two parties which I have just mentioned. I will not withdraw or qualify that statement, and if they succeed it will not be the Conservative party that will be in power but the Manufacturers' Association.
We have endeavoured to deal with the tariff to some extent, and we have pointed out some of the reasons for the falling off in revenue. Hon. gentlemen opposite and especially the ex-Miniister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) seemed to be very much concerned at the present time over the workmen. The hon. member seemed to be able to weave that word " workers " into his argument many times. I should like to ask that hon, gentleman if he has carefully considered the tariff revisions and what is the largest item in the whole tariff list of reductions. If the workers of this country are to succeed, the first essential is a reduction in the high cost of living. The largest item in the whole list of tariff reductions which became effective last year
is on the importation of sausage casings which stand in the list at $55,000 as a loss of Tevenue to this country. Will my hon. friends say in this House that this duty should be restored on this article which enters into an article of food that is bought by the working man every day of the year. I do not think that they will venture such an assertion. I also wish to show that in the total imports the tariff reductions are largely in the general tariff. The next largest item to the one to which I have referred is that of agricultural machinery. But taking the tariff reductions as a whole the reductions and the loss in revenue on the general tariff amount to $15,000,000. In the preferential tariff, as I pointed out before, the amount is about the same as that of the previous year. The treaty rates which were largely criticized in this House this year and last and which we were told were not worth the paper on which they were written, have worked out splendidly and we find that the imports under the treaty arrangements of 'last year from the different countries show an increase of something over $2,000,000; or in round figures, the imports under treaty rates in 1924 amounted to $5,731,000, while for the first ten months of this year they amounted to $7,916,000. Therefore, it is obvious that the treaty arrangements that have been entered into by this government have not only worked out splendidly from the standpoint of bringing in cheaper goods, but have had the effect of increasing the revenue. As I pointed out in the first portion of my remarks, it canuot be laid at the door of this government that the reduction in the duty was the cause of loss in revenue, because it has been plainly shown, and anyone who glances over the returns will see that the great loss in revenue was due to lack of importations, and no government can force people to buy or import against their will.
A good deal of the time of the House has been taken up with a discussion of loans to the railways. As I discussed that matter somewhat fully last session, I will not trouble the House with any further remarks regarding that question. A clipping which I have in my hand referring to Sir Henry Thornton reads:.
London, June 30, 1924.
King George received the premiers of the Canadian provinces at a garden party at Buckingham Palace. In questioning the visitors on Canadian affairs, His Majesty expressed very particular pleasure at the success of Six Henry Thornton as president of the Canadian National Railways. " You have taken a good man away from us in England," said the King.
1622	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. MacLean (Prince)
I	do not think we want any higher tribute to the gentleman who is president of the Canadian National system at the present time. We have our grievances in the Maritime provinces, but the president of the road has paid us several visits and has done a great deal in the direction of remedying the situation. He has been very painstaking in every detail that has been brought to his attention, and although we have not obtained all the reductions which we had hoped for, nevertheless certain reductions have been made by means of which the Maritime provinces have |been placed on a very much better basis than in previous years. When we came into confederation we were supposed to receive certain rights but as time went on and so many different changes came about in the railway system those rights were gradually taken from us one by one until now they have almost completely disappeared. Have we ever studied the railway situation in this light? We have a great many government services in this country all of which possibly are essential; but I think hon. gentlemen will agree with me that perhaps there is no service that can be rendered. by this government which is as essential to the people of Canada tojday as the service rendered by the Canadian National Railways. We spend millions on other services; do we get any returns? We may get returns in an indirect way, but it is a very indirect way indeed; and we do not get interest on our money nor do we see the results in any very tangible form. Now here is an institution which has given to the people of Canada a service which they could not possibly have got along without. We all hope the day is not far distant when this service will be on a paying basis; but until that time comes is it any crime that some assistance should be given to the Canadian National Railways by the government of Canada? I do not think it is. Someone will say, why is it that the Canadian Pacific Railway is able to get along and pay dividends while the Canadian National Railways are hardly able to meet operating expenses? My answer to that question is this:	The Canadian Pacific
Railway built its roads into those portions of the country where dividends were in sight, whereas the Canadian National system was built into those sections of Canada that needed to be opened up so that the great hinterlands of the north might be settled. That in my opinion is the answer to such a question. The Canadian Pacific Railway went

after dividends, and in doing so they built their roads where they expected the traffic to pay. The Canadian National Railways on the other hand have up to the present time been operated in the interests of the country and if they have not been as successful as their rival the reason I think is just as I have stated.
It may not be of interest to the House to know this, but I may say that before coming to Ottawa to attend the present session I prepared at the request of the railway commissioners a brief which I submitted to the management of the Canadian National Railways in regard to reductions. We felt that we had certain grievances in Prince Edward Island which called for some remedy, and after gathering all the information that I could upon the subject I submitted this brief to the Canadian National and have received their reply. With the permission of the House, Mr. Speaker, I should like to place this statement on Hansard: It is most interesting to the people of the Maritime provinces and it deals with questions affecting not only Prince Edwrard Island but also the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. The management endeavoured to meet us as best they could, and I may observe here that they have before them other items which they state will receive their careful consideration.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Dalrymple of the Canadian National Railways. The management did not meet our views altogether and as I proceed I shall explain our case as we saw it. The document is dated February 27, 1925 and reads:

The Budget-Mr. MacLean (Prince)

Traffic and Express Department Montreal, Quebec,
February 27, 1925.
At Hamilton
A. E. MacLean, Esq., M.P.
House of Commons,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Mr. MacLean :
In re Rates on Traffic-Prince Edward Island.
Your favour of February 13th, addressed to our president:
There has been some slight delay in answering the enquiries as several of the statements made were of an omnibus character and involved research.
I will, however, endeavour to answer the various complaints or comparisons in a tabulated manner, as follows:
(a)	Railway insists on consignee discharging shipments of potatoes at Charlottetown-cars to warehouse-whereas work is performed at St. John without expense to consignee.
The statement is not quite correct; it is, nevertheless, a fact that we assume the expense of unloading potatoes, in packages, when for furtherance by water. We do not assume the cost of unloading shipments in bulk.
The situation at St. John is somewhat different to that existing at Charlottetown, for the reason that the potatoes originate practically at the outskirts of Charlottetown, paying to the transportation company a minimum rate, w'hereas the commodity destined to St. John travels a much longer distance,-besides, we do not absorb the handling charges on traffic which pays a rate less than 10 cents per hundred pounds.
With the opening of next season, at Charlottetown, we will see that the feature of handling is placed on a parity with St. John.
(b)	Five days free time allowed at Charlottetown and ten days at St. John.
This is correct. The extra time allowed at St. John was for the purpose of over-coming irregularity in transportation, or. in other words, a railway disability caused by the fact that the potatoes moved for long distances, even in excess of 400 miles, whereas, at Charlottetown, the maximum distance is 117 miles. There would appear to be no good business reason for extending the time at Charlottetown and so far we have had the impression that the only reason why the extra time has been requested is for the purpose of utilizing railway equipment for storage, owing to the absence of adequate warehousing accommodation.
We are making a further investigation on this angle of the situation and are open to conviction.
(c)	Distance tariff rates on potatoes are greater than in New Brunswick to St. John.
This statement is not correct. The local rates, between all stations in the Maritime provinces, are on a mileage basis and the one distance tariff applies throughout the territory. In the case of export, the rates to both St. John and Charlottetown are precisely the same for corresponding distances, except that the rate to Charlottetown for distances 100 miles to 120 miles is held to a maximum of 13 cents, while to St. John the rates go up to 14 and 14J cents.
(d)	Wants general reduction in rates on potatoes to Sydney, Montreal, Halifax and St. John, but as Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick rates from Dominion points are on same basis as lower provinces admits this means a general reduction
[DOT] throughout Dominion.
There is quite a long answer to that question, and I think I might be allowed to put it on Hansard without reading it.

We would like to hear
it.
Mr. MaeLEAN (Prince):	My hon. friend
is interested?

Yes indeed.
Mr. MaeLEAN (Prince): I quote:
Rates on potatoes between and from points in the Maritime provinces have been subject to special consideration a great many times, during the past few years, and substantial reductions have already been made to assist the producer. The increases made since 1918, result of enhanced expenses due to things which need not be elaborated upon at this time, have, in so far as relates to potatoes for export, been entirely wiped out and in this respect the Maritime provinces have had preferential consideration.
Perhaps my hon. friend will not like to hear that.

No, I like to hear that.
I	am very glad to see it.
Mr. MaeLEAN (Prince):	Right here
I want to pay a compliment to the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens). In connection with the trip which the men from the Maritime provinces took across Canada, I think my hon. friend made the best suggestion of any that were offered. If he was correctly reported, his statement was that the remedy for the difficulties of the Maritime provinces in this regard was to bring the Maritime provinces within 300 miles of Montreal. My hon. friend has a good grasp of the situation. I wish we could reciprocate by bringing the western districts within 300 miles of that same great city. I presume he meant a subsidy.
The Maritime provinces are handicapped in that whatever products they have for export to Great Britain must very largely be shipped first to Montreal, involving a long rail haul of about 700 mlies, and then these same products are loaded on the ships at Montreal and are again brought back right past our doors. That is a tremendous tax on the farmers of the Maritime provinces, and to a certain extent it is the fault of the Maritime provinces themselves. A few years ago the suggestion was made that stoek-yards should be established somewhere in the Maritime provinces where stock for shipment across the ocean could be collected and where the buying could be done. There was this disagreement, however, among the different towns in the Maritime provinces as to where those stock-yards should be located, and in the meantime the thing went

1624	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. MacLean (Prince)
by the board and the stock-yards were never established. It seems to me, to use the words of the hon. member for St. John and Albert (Mr. Baxter) when he thundered here a few nights ago, and suggested that the government should wake up, that we in the Maritime provinces should wake up. If St. John and Halifax want to retain the export trade of the Maritime provinces it is up to them to wake up and provide the facilities and to agree with one another when any proposal of this kind is made.
The next question is as follows:
(e)	Wants potatoes carried at special or commodity rates and cites coal as a basis to shoot at and gives certain comparisons. Later advocates rates should not exceed rates on grain in western Canada.
In this connection I compared the rates on coal from the Maritime provinces to Prince Edward Island. I pointed out that it, to produce a ton of coal at the pit's mouth costs approximately $3, while it costs from $9 to $15 to produce a ton of potatoes, and that they sell at destination at about the same price. The rate on coal from Sydney to Tignish, Prince Edward Island, is 13 1-2 cents per 100 pounds, and the rate on potatoes from Tignish to Sydney is 38 cents per 100 pounds, a difference of 25 cents per 100 pounds or a preference of about 200 per cent on a commodity that costs 200 per cent less to produce. Coal has a commodity rate, and my contention in this case was that if coal was given that rate for Nova Scotia, then potatoes should get the commodity rate for Prince Edward Island. Another point brought out was that the freight on a carload of coal of 60,000 pounds, at 13 1-2 cents, delivered at Tignish, was $81, while the freight on a carload of potatoes of 60,000 pounds, at 38 cents, from Tignish to Sydney, was $228, although the values of the two carloads at destination were practically the same. Of course the railways will not take this into consideration; they say the two articles are so extremely different in character that that cannot be considered. The reference to that in this memorandum is as follows:
This proposition is so fundamentally unsound that nothing would be gained by discussing it.
In (f) we advocate general advances over the Dominion in the rates of luxuries and expensive goods, and a reduction on cheap or bulky articles. I think that is a proposition worthy of consideration. The reply to that suggestion is as follows:
In principle we quite agree with you as to advances on luxuries and expensive goods and this if consummated would have a natural tendency to enable us to reduce our rates on what we usually call basic commodities, but you will appreciate action even in

respect to the latter would be controlled, as heretofore, by the result of our expenses in operation.
(g)	Wants local rates on potatoes to St. John and Halifax reduced to same basis as export.
Reply to this is already covered by (d).
(h)	Gives reference to certain statements made by Premier Armstrong.
Premier Armstrong stated that freight rate from Kentville to Sydney, 317 miles, was 53 cents, while from Toronto to Winnipeg, 1,232 miles, it was only 55 cents. In other words, there was a difference of only 2 cents over that long distance.
Would that be on the same commodity?
Yes.
And the same year?

Yes, the
same year. Another instance was quoted in connection with the shipment of a box of tomatoes from Hantsport to Halifax. The freight charge was at the rate of $12.80 per 100 miles, while the rate from Grimsby, Ontario, to Halifax, was $2.50 per 100 miles. In his address before the dairymen's meeting Premier Armstrong declared that he wanted to "burn it into the minds" of the convention that these inequalities "could not be permitted to continue." He gave another instance of discrimination in freight rates. Now, the reply made by Mr. Dalrymple to that point was as follows:
Comparison of rates from Kentville to Sydney is made with rate from Toronto to Winnipeg, on apples. The latter took what is known as the Crowsnest agreement rate, which the railways are not willingly subscribing to, and if, because of the existence of this low Crowsnest basis of rates the railways are obliged to reduce all of their tariffs throughout the entire country to the lower level of such agreement rates then I can say to you very frankly there will not be sufficient money left to enable the transportation companies to furnish adequate service for our Canadian commerce.
(1)	Hay-Claimed should have flat rate from all stations on Prince Edward Island to Sydney, St. John and Halifax, as it loads so light to the carload that the rate to make it pay has to be out of all proportion to the value.
We will see what can be done in the matter of export rates on hay, from Prince Edward Island territory.
The next article dealt with is fox feed, which is an important commodity down there, and which should be fourth class instead of first class. He says:
These food stuffs consist of livers, beef hearts and horse meat shipped frozen and usually in refrigerator cars; same requires equal care to that of perishable traffic for human consumption, and we are decidedly of the opinion that the fox industry can well afford to pay first class rates. In fact, to use the argument contained in the papers which you were good enough to send us, this business might be classified as a luxury.
t

The Budget-Mr. MacLean (Prince)
We went on to ask for a reduction of freights on mixed carloads of potatoes and turnips and other freight from points in the province of Prince Edward Island to the mainland. In summing up he says:
It will perhaps not be amiss for me, at this time, to call your attention to what has been done in the matter of freight rate adjustments, affecting Prince Edward Island, during the past two years;-amongst other things the following are for your information-
(1)	Formerly rates were the combination of locals to and from island and main land, now all mileage tariffs applicable in the maritime provinces are on the flat main land basis with no additional charge for car ferry or narrow gauge line services. This involved considerable reduction in our revenue and without much increase in volume of tonnage.
(2)	Prince Edward Island is now on the flat Halifax and Mulgrave bases on all traffic to and from points west of Quebec,-a reduction in railway revenue.
(3)	Class rates between Prince Edward Island and territory west of Quebec have been readjusted on a lower level.
(4)	Reduced mileage scales locally in the maritime provinces, including Prince Edward Island, on potatoes, grain and products, have been made effective.

I am proud of the party to which I belong, and am exceeuingly proud of the leader of this great party, the Right Hon. Mr. Speaker, in beginning the few remarks which I intend to offer I feel that I am in a very happy position from the fact that I am not bound by the shackles of any party, and that I am free, as I have been since I entered this House, to support legislation, from whatever quarter of the House it may come, if I deem it to be in the best interest of the country, or to oppose it if in my opinion it is likely to have the opposite effect. On two
occasions since I have been a member of this House I opposed the budget, and voted against it, and on one occasion I supported it.
I am somewhat disappointed in the budget at this particular time. I was hopeful that we would get a budget something along the lines of the budget delivered in this House last session, but to my disappointment there is no evidence of any advance beyond the point reached by the budget last year. We had expected, from the statements made by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House, that last year's budget would be the death knell of protection. And this session I had expected that there would be some further reductions in the customs tariff on the necessities of life. I did not expect a slashing reduction and a complete sweep of the tariff; but I looked for something more than we have received. One feature of the budget in my opinion will not meet the views of those deeply interested in a low tariff and a freer trade between the nations that we have to deal with. I refer to the dumping clause. In this budget we have had a revision of the dumping clause. I have been looking over the budget for 1907 and have also considered the present budget. I have not a legally trained mind, I am a common man from behind the plough, but in my view when the dumping clause was introduced in 1907, goods coming into this country were valued at the regular market value in the country from which they were exported. As I understand the present revision, goods imported from other countries to Canada will be valued on the basis of the value of such goods in this country, or on the value of the goods on sale in this country. What does that mean? It simply means that if you go to a foreign country, buy goods and import them into Canada, you are forced, regardless of the customs tariff, to pay for those goods the value of the same goods in this country. For example, if I go to the United States and buy an article which is sold in that country for a hundred dollars and bring that over, when I come in contact with the Customs department I find that the selling price of those goods in Canada is a hundred and twenty dollars, with no reference to the customs; whatever customs duty might be placed on them would not matter. The result is that when I bring goods into this country, for an article which was sold in the United States at the regular market value of a hundred dollars I would be forced to pay a hundred and twenty dollars, before I would be per-
The Budget-Mr. Woods

mitted to use it after bringing it into this country.
Plus the duty.

Regardless of duty. As
I understand it, the dumping clause governs the whole protective feature of the goods coming into this country.

There is nothing in that
clause that I can see that prevents the Minister of Customs putting any value he likes on the goods.
Hear, hear.

We would not assume that he would put any higher value than the market value in this country. But assuming he puts on the same value, what does it mean? It means that the combined organization of manufacturers in this country could fix the price almost at any level and prohibit the consumer in this country importing goods from a foreign country without paying the price the same goods would cost him in this country. If I am right in that assumption, it is the most vicious form of protection that the human mind is capable of conceiving.
The debt of this country has been discussed time and again, and possibly almost every person in the country knows that we are loaded with a debt of almost two and a half billion dollars, which has to be met. It is a most unfortunate thing that we are saddled with such a burden. It appears to me that this enormous debt is a result of the lack of vision in war-time and the failure to collect from the people who were then making abundance of money. At the time the war was on, the farmers, the labourers, manufacturers and all classes of people were making a very great deal of money, and could with- ' out any inconvenience whatever have paid almost the entire war debt as the war went on. But, for lack of vision, we are saddled with this debt and we are compelled in some way or another to pay it. The question is how are we going to meet that debt. One of the ordinary methods which assists the average individual when he gets into debt, whether rightly or wrongly, is to retrench. There are two methods. The first, is to increase our revenue and bring more money into our possession with which to liquidate our debt. The other method is to retrench. In my opinion, the government of to-day is not retrenching as rapidly as it might do. There are many departments connected with the government of this country, and possibly there is no department in which there could

not be more retrenchment than there is at the present time. I am going to mention two or three departments out of the many in which there might be a cutting down of expenditures and a lessening of the estimates that go through this House. The estimates of the Department of National Defence might be cut down. I do not want to be misunderstood. I believe in a proper police force. I believe in our Royal Canadian Mounted Police and in a permanent militia to a certain extent, sufficient to look after the internal affairs of our country in case of any disturbance or need. But we have what is called the annual drill of the militia, and a considerable amount of money is spent on this. I had a little experience in my younger days in that regard, and I look upon it as almost a waste of money. A number of officers, some of whom do not take much from the revenues of this country for their sendees, take charge of the annual drill as the men go out into the various camps for one or two weeks, and some young men go out and have a fairly good time during this period. They continue that sort of thing each year for two or three years and then they are discharged. They are not trained to be soldiers, and a great number of them, as I saw them in my younger days, were not physically fit ever to make soldiers. I believe that branch of our Department of National Defence should be cut down. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) brought in a resolution regarding the defence of the Pacific coast and he stated, I think, that there was a coast line on the Pacific of about 10,000 miles to be guarded. If we are to put on a force sufficient to stand against any of the surrounding nations that possibly might rise up in war against us, that- would saddle us with another debt possibly almost equal to the one we are now carrying. When we were forced into the struggle some years ago, the Canadian people with their energy, their physical power and their willingness to defend their country, in a short time got ready an army to send overseas in defence of the British Empire. I believe a good deal could be saved by retrenching in the Department of National Defence.

The policy of the present government seems to be to increase the revenues. the duty the necessity for revenue. It appears to me now that the government should not spend all its energies in loading and re-loading the people of Canada with extra taxation to the very limit, while there is a possibility of reducing our debt by retrenchment in a great many directions.
I am more favourable to the sales tax than I am to the customs duty. The sales tax is something in regard to which we are more in the light; we know what we are paying for. Although it may be shouldered on the consumer ultimately, we know at any rate more about this tax than we do about the customs tariff and the dumping clause that protects the various industries. Personally, I prefer direct taxation; I want to know exactly what I am paying for.
Let me refer now to the stamp tax on cheques, a matter I discussed when the legislation was put through this House in the first session I was here. At that time the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) fixed the maximum at $2 but the following session he reduced it to SI. As I see this stamp tax, all it means is that the wealthy men of this country who are able to put their signature to cheques of over $2,500 will be exempt from a tax which others will have to pay. The tax now is 2 cents for every $50 or fraction of $50 up to. $2,500, but above that sum it does not apply. It looks to me therefore as if we are legislating in the interests of the rich people of this country, and it borders very closely if not entirely on class legislation.
I want to touch for a moment now on protection, which has been the great cry of our friends to the right. One thing that has surprised me in this respect is that hon. gentlemen to our right have not put this principle in the form of a platform, as the hon. member for Kings (Mr. Hughes) observed last night, when he said that certain resolutions contained the issues upon which the Conservative party were likely to go to the country. Hon. members to my right moved an amendment to the budget and I must say that it strikes me as being very meaningless; it is not a resolution from which we can extract very much. So far as I can see, their amendment is not a policy at all. But if, as the hon. member said last night, our friends are going to go to the country and appeal to the people on a certain platform, it is a mystery to me at any rate why they have not submitted it to the House in the form of an amendment to the budget with a view to having it threshed out on the floor. Why do they not want to bring it to the attention of the
The Budget-Mr. Woods

people as coming direct from the Parliament of Canada? Were hon. gentlemen timid, were they a little bit afraid to launch out on the great sea of protection in this way? At any rate, they seem to be holding back until some future time when no doubt they will bring forward their policy on the hustings. Now, protection does not always protect, and in this regard I want to read a brief statement I clipped from the public press written by Mr. Tom King who is the correspondent of the Globe at Washington and who writes in this instance touching the situation in the United States. We are told that there is a high protective tariff over there, and this perhaps is true in the case of a great many articles. But this is what that gentleman says about the situation as he sees it:
The United States farmers already have tariff protection, but a customs wall is useless to producers of wheat, corn, cotton and hogs. They have a surplus for export and must take prices fixed in the world's market.
What is true of the United States is also true of Canada. We are a large agricultural nation and we are producing in excess, by millions of bushels, of what we can consume in wheat. Of hogs, cattle and farm produce we also have an excess of production over consumption; and as we must place those prodilcts on the markets of the world in competition with other countries, protection does not avail us very much. And this is the same in the United States. So that protection does not always protect.
Personally I am not a free trader; I never believed in absolute free trade so long as we were up against a tariff wall in other countries. But I do not believe in retaliation, and I do not believe that it would be wise for a moment for Canada to put up a tariff wall against the United States or any other country simply because they excluded our products in that way. I do not think however that we ought to regulate our tariff; we should regulate the duties on the necessities of life, in the interests of the masses. We should not make things harder for the general public by increasing the cost of living and so driving the people out of the country. I believe therefore that it is our duty to regulate our tariff with the principle in view of the greatest good to the greatest number and not in the interests of any class or small section of the people.
There is another point I would like to touch upon-and I am not sure that it is not a delicate one in some respects; I do not know what view my western friends who sit around me hold in regard to it. But following the idea that I have just expressed of doing the greatest good to the greatest number, my

opinion is that the government would be acting wisely if it put an export duty on wheat. Let me give you my reasons. I have said that protection does not always protect, and that we have to put our surplus produce on the world's market. But the United States to-day has a protective tariff of forty-two cents a bushel against our Canadian wheat, and the result is that the millers of the United States buy our wheat, take it over to their mills in that country, mill it and export it. I am informed on good authority that when they export it they get the benefit of a drawback to the extent of 99 per cent of the duty paid. The duty that the United States has put against Canadian wheat does not help the farmers there but it does benefit the great milling companies of the United States, while it injures the millers of our own country. If our wheat was milled in our own country we would get the benefit of the byproducts for feed, and we all know how necessary those by-products are in such a province as Ontario. We must have them for the feeding of young stock and in connection with our dairy operations. But when the United States get our wheat and export it, with practically no tariff charge when you consider the drawback of 99 per cent, our milling industries are preventing from handling it and sending it over to Great Britain in the form of flour, and we are deprived of the use of the by-products for our young stock and for dairy feed.

Before the hon. member gets away from that, has he thought out what effect an export duty would have on the sale of our wheat in Europe? Would it not drive the Canadian exporter off the markets of the world? You cannot put an export duty against the United States without putting it on also against Europe.

Well, it might have some effect in that way, but it would build up our milling industries and give us the by-products. Whether rightly or wrongly, I cannot help thinking that it would be a wise thing to do, because it would operate very much in the interests of this country; it would bring a great deal of revenue into the treasury and would help pay off our national debt as well as give us the other benefits that I have described.

That is right. Now, I want to refer to a statement made recently in this House by the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion). Referring to the present condition of affairs in Canada with regard to employment and so on, he said that he had never known it to be so bad. He went a little further and said that from bis knowledge of history he had never known it to be so bad; that such a serious state of affairs had not existed since the period between 1873 and 1878. Now, perhaps I will be pardoned if I tell the House something cf the conditions between 1878 and the close
of the century, based on actual experience. In the latter part of the eighties and possibly all through the eighties, and in the early nineties, conditions to my mind, and I came through them, were much worse than they are at the present time. I was actively engaged in farming in the early nineties and part of the eighties. I was in the working class, and knew considerable about the conditions in 1878, and onward; so much so that I was interested in politics at that particular time while still a young man, and I was then a very ardent supporter, I must confess, of the policy of Sir John A. Macdonald, which our friends to my right always advocate. In the early nineties the farmers could hire a man on the farm for S15 and $16 a month. The farmers at that time received about $4 a hundred for dressed hogs, and about $3 to $3.50 a hundred for live hogs. They could sell beef cattle that had been stable fed for six months at a price-I was going to say at the enormous price of 4 cents or 4} cents a pound. I came through that particular period and have had actual experience of these conditions; I am speaking of Ontario; I do not know anything about the other provinces. I have had the actual experience in this province of selling dressed hogs, beautiful carcasses, for $4 a hundred, and of selling in May beef cattle that had been stable fed all winter for $4 a hundred. These were the conditions back in the nineties, when as I say we could hire our men for $15 and $16 a month. Compare that with conditions to-day. Hired men to-day on the farms in our locality and round about are getting from $30 to $40 and in some cases $43 a month the year round, and their board. In some cases they have a horse fed for them, and they have the opportunity of driving out with their own horse and rig supplied by the farmer, in addition to getting $40 a month the year round. There was no horse fed for them in the early nineties, and they were then only getting $15 and $16 a month. To-day while the farmers have difficulties to contend with, and high prices generally, we can sell live hogs at $12 and $13 a hundred, and beef cattle at from $6 to $8 a hundred in the province of Ontario. Of course, we may have got into a little extravagant way of living, which is all right in its place if we have the means to do it, but conditions to-day make it far easier to live on the same plane, and to have as few "outings" so to speak, than they did in the eighties and nineties, under this great protects ive policy, this panacea for all our ailments, that was launched in 1878 as the great National Policy for the Dominion of Canada.

Now, I want to refer to another point and that is that protection is driving small industries out of the country. I believe the protective policy has had more to do with driving small industries from our towns and villages than anything else which has taken place in Canada. It has depopulated the rural sections of the Dominion and is forcing the young men and women, and other workers, into the large centres. Then when conditions are not favourable in those centres they cross to the country to the south to look for employment there. At any rate I am convinced of the fact that protection has done more to break up our small towns and villages and to destroy our small industries than any other agency.
Now I am going to relate a condition which came to my notice very recently which, I think, will prove conclusively the statement I have made. It is a condition that was brought to my attention by some of the fence manufacturing companies of the province of Ontario, and it is this: The Canadian fence companies that weave wire fences for the farmers import certain lines of wire free of duty, and I approve of the Canadian manufacturers obtaining their raw material duty free because it should lower their production costs and enable them t-o put their products on the market at a reduced price. The companies that manufacture woven wire fences have the privilege of going into the open market buying No. 9, No. 12 and No. 13 wire and importing it free of duty. There is a No. 10 wire which is a Shade lighter wire than No. 9, but which still makes a very good fence. There are, as far as I know, only two large companies in Canada that manufacture steel wire for fencing, and they also manufacture fences out of No. 10 wire. They import their raw material free for the manufacture of that wire, and they put their fences woven from No. 10 wire on the market in competition with fences woven from No. 9 wire, selling them as a light No. 9 wire fence or as a standard gauge wire fence. Now, the other companies that weave wire fences do not manufacture the wire. They can go to these two particular companies and buy No. 9, No. 12, and No. 13 wire at practically the same price at which they can buy it across the line and bring it into Canada; but when it is a case of getting No. 10 wire, which is protected by a 20 per cent duty, these two particular companies manufacturing this wire
say to the other companies "We will give you that wire at so much" which represents the 20 per cent duty added to the price. It is a prohibitive price for other manufacturers desirous of weaving fences from No. 10 wire. So these two companies enjoying this special advantage sell No. 10 wire at a price fifty cents higher than the other companies who sell No. 9 wire fences and they also sell No.
9 wire as well. Now fencing in this country is a very important matter not only for the farmers on the western prairies but elsewhere in Canada. Fences made from No. 10 wire can be put on the market only by these two favoured companies; the other concerns are prohibited from weaving and selling No. 10 wire fence by the addition of the 20 per cent duty. What is going to be the result of this? The result will be to drive out the other woven wire fence companies and to give a monopoly of the business to the two companies that manufacture the wire and also turn out woven wire fences, but who are selling fences made from No. 10 wire at fifty cents a hundred higher than they sell fences made from No. 9 wire. That concrete case has been brought to my attention. I have laid the matter before the government, and they say it was an bid thing and has been there for years; but I am hopeful that the government of the day will remove that discrimination against the small manufacturer in favour of the larger manufacturers of wire and fencing.

The Liberals outwitted them, went over to the United States and stole the Conservative platform. We know that the Conservative policy back in the eighties and nineties was that as soon as the United States was willing to put the natural products of the country on the free list Canada would do the same, and that we would have reciprocity in the natural products of the country. Mr. Speaker, the budget speech, this year, affords to the citizens of this country the satisfaction and joy of noticing a marked improvement in our finances. For a long time to come, we shall look forward with much anxiety to the yearly budget statement of the Minister of Finance, because we shall bear in mind the never to be forgotten days of the Great War, the sacrifices we bore up with and the heavy obligations incurred. These war oebts must be met. The word of honour and pledges of our predecessors must be scrupulously adhered to. Therefore, this year as in previous years the Acting Minister of Finance rightly stated:
However, upon the Dominion treasury had fallen the cost of our share in the war, the interest on the war debt, the pensions to our disabled soldiers and to the widows and orphans of our men who had fallen at the front. The present government, representing the will of the Canadian people, has constantly borne in mind the debt we owe to the disabled and the needs of the widows and orphans, which necessitated pension increases from year to year.
We therefore have cause to rejoice that the government has managed the affairs of the country with such foresight and economy that, after having discharged in full the heavy debts, which were a consequence of the war, and met the needs of the hour, it can bring down a budget which shows a favourable balance. The latter is the result of a wise administration. 1 he government first of all deserves our confidence on the score of wise economy. The statement of the Minister of Finance will be received with much satisfaction by the electors. Among other things the minister said:
On the other hand, by reductions in general expenditures and by refinancing maturing loans, the government has succeeded in reducing the interest charges and also our annual expenditures, thus enabling us last year to report a material reduction in our net debt and this year a substantial reduction in taxation and a surplus in the government's own administrative services.
The government's financial transactions may thus be summed up: debt decrease, taxation decrease, expenditure decrease and a favourable balance in this year's budget.
This financial success of the government is the vindication of the people of this country

The Budget-Mr. Fortier
who have entrusted the Liberal party with the ship of state. Had the government to its credit but this record of restoring the finances on a sound basis, it would be entitled to the confidence and gratitude of those who had entrusted to it the task of working for the reconstruction of the country shaken by the war. Deeds speak more eloquently than high sounding words or great promises. What did the people expect, in 1921, from the government? The post-war reconstruction, the balancing of our finances. The latter has just been done by the Minister of Finance. He has established this favourable balance notwithstanding a decrease in taxation, that is to say, in the revenue, although refunding more than $35,000,000 of the national debt. I do not know when we shall be called upon to go before the electors so as to obtain their endorsation of the acts of this government, but I feel certain that no administrative acts will commend themselves more to the consideration, the confidence and respect of the people than the great concern of our leaders to re-establish equilibrium in our finances. However, the management of our national railways will be the source, for some years to come, of considerable deficits as well as capital outlay necessitated by the improvements and equipment of the railway. However, we cannot do otherwise than shoulder all the responsibilities of said management which we have not sought, but that we have accepted with the solemn promise to give it a fair trial.
Discussing the chances of success of the State management of industries, in France the champions of this system assure us of good results, providing however that the undertaking be left in the hands of a permanent and responsible chief. The government was fortunate in entrusting the management of our National railways to Sir Henry Thornton. Indeed, since he was chosen president of the railway board, Sir Henry has carried out great improvements to the National railways. This railway ownership is to the advantage of our country and helps wonderfully to the development of the newer parts of the country and to the spreading of the population. I have the honour to represent in parliament a settlement, where for more than twenty-five years, the sturdy settlers have gradually conquered the virgin forests to establish on the mountain slopes and in all the valleys of the Rouge and Lievre rivers the flourishing farms and numerous parishes which make up a wonderful landscape in the Laurentian mountains. So as to meet the needs of the settlers, accommodate these far off settlements and open up the back country, the railway has
become an indispensable thing. It has always been' a wise policy for our federal as well as provincial governments, to grant to private companies the necessary subsidies to induce the latter to build railways through those settlements. But do these private companies, even encouraged by these various grants always meet the needs of those districts? Do they not often require subsidies representing a considerable proportion of the cost of construction? This being the case, would it not be wiser for the government to build themselves the railway rather than supply the funds to have them built by others and for others.
Railways, however, are so necessary to the exploitation of natural resources and the reasonable development of our country, that it would be expedient to complete, as circumstances would warrant, the National railways and to subsidize, when necessary private companies willing to build branch lines. At all events, we should congratulate ourselves in possessing a national railway which furthers so well the development and expansion of our young country, and we should not fear, for some time to come, the adverse financial situation which government ownership creates.
I realize that in certain quarters, these contentions may be challenged. Commercial centres, large cities do not feel the need, as settlements directly interested in the construction of branch lines do, of continuing state-ownership. Those who receive excellent service do not generally wish for more. But as their hopes, however, turn towards other fields of vantage, they seek for such ends funds which are otherwise invested. Let me point out to you that commercial centres and large cities have come in existence through these means of communication and in particular through these railways which link them with outside points, with neighbouring or far off regions, and which contribute largely to the wonderful development of trade and industry. The great voice of cities should equally mingle their appeals to that of those parts to be developed so as to support the claims of our rural districts for the extension of our railways.

The Minister of Finance has given us a glimpse of the dawn of a brighter day in the revival of activities which agriculture seems to display. He says:
But there is a bright spot. Agricultural industries, especially in the prairie provinces, are now receiving the benefits of greatly increased prices for last year's crops, and these increased revenues are being applied, not to luxuries or comforts, but to wiping off the indebtedness incurred during the lean years. The farm, free from debt, brings more general economic value to the owner and to Canada as a whole.
Now, agriculture is the oldest, the noblest and the most remunerating of all industries. Why do we give such prominence to agriculture? It is because we are aware that it is in this industry that humanity has its fountain-head of life. While all other industries confine themselves to transforming the raw materials of which they only utilize a part, agriculture multiplies its raw materials, increases them tenfold or even a hundredfold. The sun is its great assistant in this work of creation. Agriculture is therefore one of the main branches of human activity, it is the oldest. Fenelon says that, "agriculture which is the basis of life, is the source of real worldly goods." It has always been looked upon of such importance that all the ancient traditions agree in giving it a divine origin. The notion that we have formed of agriculture, in Quebec, is that it cannot be progressive or remunerative unless it has as its basis the dairy industry. When fifty years ago, the country was suffering under a general depression and it was in the throes of a most serious economic crisis, what was the remedy proposed? Our clergy, our statesmen rose and proclaimed an agricultural crusade. They founded, in 1882, a dairymen's association and they spread throughout all the parishes this truth: that the dairy industry is the principal means of salvation for the farm.	Our fathers will bear
witness to the fact.	It is the dairy industry which saved us from ruin; it enriched the farm, the homestead, by first paying off the mortgage and by restoring to the soil its original fertility.
In what other parts more than in those old provinces of the Dominion, is it necessary to always proclaim that the dairy industry is indispensable to agricultural development. In our parishes economic conditions may be gauged by the state the farm values stand in direct ratio to the number of well

equipped and well managed butter and cheese factories as well as to the high quality of the herds. In the interesting settlements which I have the honour to represent we realize that the example of prosperous agricultural centres must be followed, and that is why this industry has had such an awakening. Is it not there that dairy industry is most needed to complete and consolidate the national work of colonization performed by our worthy and heroic pioneers.
To retain these energetic sons on the Canadian soil, to keep the settler with us, to offer him as well as to his repatriated fellow-citizen, new lands to settle upon, that is. the policy which thrills with enthusiasm the heart of those who love their province. I call as witnesses those who were the great servants of our country. Does not one read on the pedestals of Cartier's monument, the advice which he gave to his fellow citizens and which he expressed in these simple words, "Let us take possession of the soil." Let us listen to this other congenial voice, that of Manager Labelle, the apostle of colonization: "It is absolutely necessary"-he repeated to the pioneers he had settled in the new parishes-"that you devote your time to the development of your primitive clearings so as to make of these wonderful northern lands, watered by rivers and lakes, the excellent pastures which will make of your region the Switzerland of Canada."
Great and numerous are the advantages which the dairy industry brings to our farms. The land is bare and desolate when it is not stocked with a fine herd. And does it not seem to you that the landscape is more picturesque, farming life more charming and attractive when you discover on the hills or the plains, in the midst of extensive grazing lands, a magnificent herd of milch-cows. Their variegated colourings bring joy to one's heart. Every evening they slowly wind their way towards the home bringing to the family the best, the richest, the healthiest food: the good and unadulterated milk.
But this hope of a new dawn, through the revival of agriculture, would shine with a brighter light, if the government had been allowed to realize its policy of new markets for the output of our products. These markets are necessary to hasten larger production and to sell at profitable prices, all the products of our farming industry.
What we need, is a trade convention with our neighbours to the south, so as to allow us to export on that market, which is the natural and best outlet that we can hope for, our farm products suitable for exportation.

I have faith in the future and believe in the destinies of our party which the Canadian people will return to power at the next general election. I hope that the voting, by testifying to a greater confidence in the policy of our government, will allow them to realize this programme of trade intercourse with the United States, so as to favour the Canadian farm and, thereby, bring to this country a better economic situation.
Now, it is with the aim of reaching, with greater facility, the so necessary markets that the government has concluded a contract with English shippers so as to control and reduce the excessive freight charges on our exports to Europe.	The government acted
wisely for, in the Petersen contract, they showed both desire to meet the needs of the hour, by striking at the transportation trust, and the prudence which must attend such a vast undertaking.	The government critics
willingly admitted the need of breaking up the trust, but they fear that the project will not serve the ends sought. If their contentions are right, those yearly subsidies during the progress of the contract are the most economic, because in case of failure, they will prove the less expensive, providing that when this contract terminates we shall be free from all future responsibilities.
In closing my remarks I wish to congratulate the government on its praiseworthy effort to better our economic situation. The government have understood that it is by these means which I have just pointed out, and by others also, which they unflinchingly put into practice, that they may reach their goal. Let me remark, by the way, that in order to carry the burden of the debt and those obligations which are summed up in the taxes, we must necessarily adopt such means as to make a more general assessment of taxes. However, this assessment cannot be carried out -with the present population. We must, therefore, increase our numbers.
It is with that aim in view that the government has adopted a sound immigration and repatriation policy. And, in order that this immigration be controlled, we must require at the port of embarkation a certificate from the immigrant establishing that he is sound of body and mind. It is a prudent and wise move to restrict the number of these ports of embarkation so as to stimulate a healthy immigration flowing from Belgium, France, Switzerland, the Scandinavian countries and the British Empire, and it will do away with many quite justifiable prejudices against unrestricted immigration.
And, to stem the emigration of our people, we have but to continue the policy so well established by the government which consists in obtaining all the advantages possible so as to encourage the Canadians to make their home on the land and help them in settling and farming.
In realizing the beginning of this task of restoration accomplished by the government since they are in power, I publicly reiterate my confidence in them. And I state that it is with pleasure that I shall support with my vote the budget which has just been delivered with such ability and eloquence by the !hon. Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb).
